_formatting_readme: FORMATTING RULE for this file and hwr-websites.json: every object that lives inside an array (each hubNav entry, each categories entry, each page's section entry in 'sections', and every site entry in hwr-websites.json) must be written as ONE single line of compact JSON -- not one key per line. Only the record itself is collapsed; the surrounding array/object indentation stays normal (2 spaces per level, same as the rest of this file). See any existing entry below for the exact style to match. If you are an AI editing this file: when you add, edit, or regenerate any array of objects here, keep this one-line-per-record format -- do not let a formatter/pretty-printer expand records back out to one key per line.
_hubNav_readme: Drives BOTH the mobile bottom nav bar (.bn-bar / #bottomNav) and the desktop 'Web Resources' hub strip (.stb-hub-nav / #stbHubNav) — the same 4 (or however many you list) destinations, built once here and shared by every hwr-*.html page via 11layout.js. Add, remove, reorder, rename, re-link, or re-icon an entry here and it updates everywhere automatically — no HTML editing needed on any page. On mobile, entries are split around the floating 'More' button: the first half render before it, the rest after (e.g. 4 items = 2 + More + 2); this split happens automatically based on how many entries you have. Which entry shows as 'active' is no longer hand-coded per page — 11layout.js compares each entry's 'link' against the current page's own filename and highlights whichever one matches (none light up on pages that aren't one of these destinations, e.g. /web-resources/ai-tools).

_hubNav_fields.name: Label shown under/next to the icon.
_hubNav_fields.link: Destination page (bare filename, e.g. '/web-resources/bookmarks') — also what's compared against the current page to decide the active state.
_hubNav_fields.icon: Inner SVG markup (just the <path>/<circle>/etc children, no outer <svg> tag) for this item's NORMAL/inactive state. Same format as every other icon in this file — see '_icon_style_guide' below. Rendered at 24x24, fill='none', stroke='currentColor'.
_hubNav_fields.activeIcon: Optional. Inner SVG markup for this item's ACTIVE state (shown when 'link' matches the current page) — lets you use a genuinely different/solid icon instead of just recoloring the outline one. Bake any fill directly into the markup itself (e.g. fill='currentColor' on the shape, fill='none' on any stroke-only detail that must stay hollow, like Contribute's '+') rather than relying on outside CSS, so the active icon renders correctly no matter where it's reused. If omitted, the normal 'icon' is reused for the active state too.

_featured_readme: Cards in the scrolling strip on /web-resources/, rendered by initFeaturedMarquee(). Order here is the order they scroll in. The strip duplicates this list once at runtime to make the loop seamless — never duplicate entries by hand. Fields mirror hwr-websites.json so a card can be copied straight across; "cat" only drives the small category tag on the card.
_sections_readme: Each key below is a page's filename (must match the <script> lookup of location.pathname on that page). The value is an ordered list of that page's 'Table of Contents' sections — each one becomes BOTH a numbered row in the sidebar TOC card AND a heading + card-list + 'View All' button in the main content column. To add a new page (e.g. Movies), copy the '/web-resources/ai-tools' array below, rename the key to '/web-resources/movies', and edit each entry's id/title/group/containerId to match that page's own categories — no HTML editing needed on the page itself, it reads straight from this file.

_section_fields.id: Slug used to build the anchor id (toc-<id>) that TOC rows link to and section headings scroll to. Must be unique within the page.
_section_fields.title: Display name shown in both the sidebar TOC row and the section heading above its card list.
_section_fields.group: Must exactly match the 'group' value used on that site's entries inside hwr-websites.json — this is how cards get sorted into the right section.
_section_fields.containerId: Id given to the section's card-list <div>. Must be unique on the page (convention: <pagePrefix> + PascalCase group + 'List', e.g. aiOfficialList).
_section_fields.icon: Inner SVG markup (just the <path>/<circle>/etc children, no outer <svg> tag) for this section's icon. Source it from the Lucide icon set (lucide.dev) — pick the closest matching Lucide icon and paste in its inner path data unmodified, rather than hand-drawing new shapes, so every icon shares Lucide's exact proportions and corner geometry. Rendered at 24x24 viewBox, stroke='currentColor', fill='none'. Note: the markup's own stroke-width attribute (1.75) is overridden by CSS at render time — see '_icon_style_guide' below for the real value and the reasoning. The same icon is reused in 3 places per section: the desktop sidebar TOC row, the mobile 'More' sheet TOC row, and the big section heading above its cards. Each page's sections should get their own icon set relevant to that page's own categories (e.g. Anime's sections will need their own icons, not these AI ones).
_section_fields.noCardList: Optional, defaults to false. Set true for a section whose content is hand-authored directly in the page's HTML (e.g. the AI Tools Glossary) rather than pulled from hwr-websites.json by group. When true: 'group'/'containerId'/'subtitle' are not required and are ignored; the PAGE SECTIONS script still builds this section's TOC row (sidebar 'On This Page', mobile More-sheet, Browse Settings dropdown) and lets the scroll-spy pick it up like any other section — it just skips generating a heading/card-list/'View All' button and count badge for it, since that markup already exists by hand elsewhere on the page. The section's 'id' must still match the 'toc-<id>' anchor id already present on that hand-authored block in the HTML.

_icon_style_guide: STYLE RULES FOR EVERY 'icon' VALUE IN THIS FILE — read this before writing or editing any icon, so new ones render identically to existing ones instead of standing out. (1) SOURCE: pull the icon from Lucide (lucide.dev), matching the section's meaning as closely as possible — do not invent custom shapes; Lucide's consistent 24x24 grid, 2px corner radius, and stroke geometry is what keeps every icon in this file visually related to each other. (2) FORMAT: paste only the inner children (<path>, <circle>, <rect>, <line>, etc.) with no outer <svg> wrapper, no fill/stroke/viewBox attributes on the children themselves — those are all supplied by the wrapping <svg> that hwrSectionIconSvg() builds around whatever you put here (viewBox='0 0 24 24', fill='none', stroke='currentColor', stroke-linecap='round', stroke-linejoin='round'). (3) STROKE-WIDTH — IMPORTANT, DON'T MATCH LUCIDE'S DEFAULT: Lucide ships at stroke-width 2, and this file's icon markup itself still carries stroke-width='1.75' as a leftover attribute, but NEITHER is what actually renders. The page's CSS rule '.layouts-title-icon { stroke-width: 2.4; }' overrides both, because the icon sits directly beside a font-weight:900 uppercase title (Orbitron) and anything thinner than ~2.4 reads as frail/mismatched next to that much heavier type — this was a deliberate fix after the default weight looked wrong in practice. When writing a brand-new icon from scratch (i.e. not copying an existing Lucide shape verbatim), draw its strokes assuming they'll render at 2.4, not 1.75 or 2 — avoid tightly-packed thin details that would clot together at that heavier weight. (4) SOLID ACCENTS: small filled dots/accents inside an icon (e.g. a lens dot, a pulse dot) should use fill='currentColor' stroke='none' on that one element, same pattern as the existing voice-changer and audio-generation icons — keeps the accent crisp instead of getting the 2.4 outline stroke applied to it too. (5) SIZE: never set width/height/viewBox in the icon string itself — sizing is controlled entirely by the CSS class on whichever wrapper uses it (layouts-title-icon, nav-chip-icon, hero-tag-icon, etc.), so the same icon scales correctly in all 3 reuse locations without edits. EXCEPTION: the 4 hubNav icons are NOT Lucide on purpose -- they are a custom two-tone set (active = white main shape + a 55%-opacity grey part) matching the Clash pages' nav icons (HUB_ICONS in /coc/town-hall-18/layouts), and they carry their own fill/stroke attributes. Keep them in that style.

glossary._glossary_readme: Each key under 'pages' is a page's filename (matches the 'sections' keys above). 'title' and 'subtitle' are the exact text already hand-authored in that page's glossary heading (<div class="layouts-title-box" id="toc-<x>-glossary">) -- kept here only as a reference copy, not re-rendered by the GLOSSARY script. What the GLOSSARY script DOES read is 'terms': it builds the <dl id="glossaryList"> item list from it and writes its length into that heading's <span class="layouts-count"> badge, so adding, editing, or removing a term here is the only edit needed -- no HTML editing on the page itself. Terms stay ordered from most commonly-encountered/basic to more technical (not alphabetical), matching how a newcomer would want to read them. 'term' and 'def' are plain text with no HTML tags -- any special character (e.g. an em dash or the ¾ symbol) is written as the literal character, not an HTML entity, since the script inserts both with textContent.

/web-resources/ai-tools.title: AI Tools Glossary
/web-resources/ai-tools.subtitle: Plain-language definitions for the AI terms used across this site and beyond.

terms.def: The text you type to tell an AI what you want it to do.
A prompt written to trick an AI into ignoring its safety rules.
A small piece of a word that AI models read and write in. Limits and pricing are counted in tokens, not words.
When an AI makes something up and states it as fact.
Large Language Model: an AI trained on huge amounts of text to read and write language. ChatGPT and Claude are LLMs.
An AI that can take several steps and use tools on its own to finish a job, instead of just answering one question.
Details an AI keeps about you between chats, so you do not have to repeat yourself.
How much text an AI can hold in mind at once. Go past it and the oldest parts of the chat are forgotten.
Hidden instructions from the app that set how the AI behaves, separate from what you type.
An AI that handles more than text, such as images, audio, or video.
A setting for how creative an AI's answers are. Low is safe and predictable, high is more varied.
Extra training that makes an existing AI better at one specific job.
Retrieval-Augmented Generation: the AI looks things up in real documents before answering instead of relying on memory alone.
Text or images turned into numbers, so a computer can measure how similar two things are.
The method behind most AI image generators. It starts with random noise and slowly cleans it into a picture.
Using AI to make an image or video larger and sharper by inventing the extra detail.

/web-resources/anime.title: Anime Glossary
/web-resources/anime.subtitle: Plain-language definitions for anime fan terms and general streaming terms used across this site and beyond.

terms.def: The anime keeps its Japanese audio and you read the translation on screen.
The Japanese voices are replaced with a translated recording, usually English.
An episode with no subtitles and no dub, just the original Japanese.
An episode subtitled and streamed right after it airs in Japan, instead of months later.
Extra episodes not in the manga, added so the anime does not catch up to it. You can skip them without missing the story.
One season of about 12 episodes. A 2-cour show runs for roughly 24.
An episode released straight to disc or digital instead of airing on TV.
An anime made for online release instead of TV.
A genre where the hero is sent or reborn into another world, usually a fantasy one.
Anime aimed at teen boys, usually action-heavy. Naruto and One Piece are the classics.
Anime aimed at teen girls, built on romance and feelings. Sailor Moon is the classic.
Anime aimed at adult men. Usually darker and slower than shounen.
Anime aimed at adult women, with more realistic relationships than shoujo.
A genre about giant piloted robots, like Gundam and Evangelion.
A character who acts cold to hide the fact that they care.
A character whose love turns obsessive and dangerous.
A character who seems cold and calm but shows they care through actions.
A character who is shy and quiet until they trust you, then opens up.
A fictional character a fan adores and jokingly calls their ideal partner.
A Japanese voice actor. Many have large fanbases of their own.
The opening and ending theme songs that play at the start and end of an episode.
A short stretch of much better animation, usually saved for big fights or emotional scenes.
How much video data is sent each second. Higher means a sharper picture but needs faster internet.
The pause while a video loads more data, usually because your internet cannot keep up.
How many pixels make up the picture, like 720p or 1080p. More pixels means more detail.
Softsubs can be turned off or swapped for another language. Hardsubs are burned into the video and are always there.
A backup link or server for the same episode. Try it when the main one is slow or blocked.
A block on what you can watch based on your country, caused by licensing deals.
An app that routes your connection through another country, often used to reach blocked content.

/web-resources/asian-drama.title: Asian Drama Glossary
/web-resources/asian-drama.subtitle: Plain-language definitions for the drama fandom and streaming terms used across this site and beyond.

terms.def: When you start rooting for the second lead instead of the main couple. Almost every drama fan gets it.
A Korean TV series, usually one complete season rather than a show renewed for years.
A Chinese or Taiwanese drama. These often run 40 to 60 episodes in one season.
A Japanese drama. Some fans use the word loosely for any East Asian series.
A drama set in the past, usually with royal courts and palace politics. Some follow real history, some just borrow the setting.
A wild plot turn like a secret sibling or sudden amnesia, used purely to keep you hooked.
A member of a rich family that runs a huge business empire. A very common drama character.
Filming episodes only days before they air. Writers can react to fans, but the ending often feels rushed.
The songs written for a drama, usually released while it is still airing.
An episode with no subtitles yet, uploaded soon after it airs.
A drama subtitled and watchable almost as soon as it airs at home.
Subtitles kept as a separate track, so you can turn them off or change the language.
Subtitles burned into the video. You cannot turn them off, but they always display correctly.
A backup copy of a video on another site, useful when the main link dies.
A block on what you can stream based on your country, caused by licensing deals.
An app that routes your connection through another country, commonly used to get past geo-restrictions.
The pause while a video loads more data, usually from a slow connection.
How sharp a video is, measured in pixels like 720p or 1080p. Higher is clearer but heavier to stream.
How much data a video uses each second. Higher usually looks better but needs faster internet.

/web-resources/games.title: Gaming Glossary
/web-resources/games.subtitle: Plain-language definitions for gaming terms used across this site and beyond.

terms.def: A game repackaged into a smaller download.
A modified game file that removes copy protection so the game runs without a license.
Downloadable Content: extra levels or items released after launch, usually sold separately.
A small update that fixes bugs or changes features without reinstalling the game.
Frames Per Second: how many images your screen draws each second. Higher looks smoother.
The delay between your action and the server noticing it, in milliseconds. Lower is better.
A player-made change or addition to a game, from a small tweak to whole new content.
Software that imitates another console so you can play its games on your computer.
A copy of a game's data, played through an emulator instead of the original console.
A game you can buy and play before it is finished, while it is still being updated.
A seeder uploads a finished file to others. A leecher is still downloading it.
A save file kept online, so your progress follows you to another device.
Reloading an earlier save over and over to undo a bad result.
Non-Playable Character: anyone in the game not controlled by a real person.
Finishing a game as fast as possible, often using set routes and glitches.
Software that detects and blocks cheating, sometimes needing deep access to your system.
Good Game: said at the end of a match, win or lose.
An update that makes something weaker because it was too strong.
An update that makes something stronger. The opposite of a nerf.
Repeating the same task over and over to gain levels, gear, or money.
The strategies, builds, and characters currently considered strongest.
Sitting in one good spot instead of moving around the map.
Deliberately ruining the game for other players instead of playing properly.
Which player or enemy a hostile character is currently attacking.
A delay between what you do and what happens on screen, usually a slow connection or busy server.
The invisible shape around a character that decides whether an attack hits.
A paid in-game box that gives random rewards instead of something you choose.
The three main team roles: soaking up damage, dealing damage, and healing.
When the whole team dies at once and the fight restarts from the beginning.
A skilled player using a new account to face much weaker opponents.

/web-resources/manga.title: Manga Glossary
/web-resources/manga.subtitle: Plain-language definitions for the manga terms used across this site and beyond.

terms.def: A chapter scanned, translated, and lettered by fans rather than the publisher. It is why untranslated series appear online at all.
A chapter in its original language, before anyone translates it.
An official English chapter released the same day as the original, instead of months later.
All three mean comics, just from different countries: manga is Japanese, manhwa is Korean, manhua is Chinese.
A comic made to be scrolled straight down on a phone, usually in color. Most are Korean.
A book that collects several chapters of a series into one edition.
One installment of a series, usually 15 to 45 pages.
A complete story told in a single chapter, with no sequel planned.
A genre where the hero is pulled out of normal life and dropped into another world, often with game-like rules.
Labels for who a manga is aimed at: shonen is teen boys, shojo teen girls, seinen adult men, josei adult women.
A genre about romance between male characters. Also called yaoi.
A genre about romance between female characters. Also called yuri.
A short illustrated novel for teens and young adults. Many anime and manga start here.
The creator of a manga, who usually both writes and draws it.
The dot patterns used for shading in black-and-white manga, instead of real gray.
Most manga is read right to left, the opposite of Western books, because that is the original Japanese order.
A backup copy of a site at a different web address, for when the main one is down or blocked.
A block on what you can read based on your country, caused by licensing deals.
An app that routes your connection through another country, used to get past blocks and add privacy.
How much detail a scanned page holds. A low-resolution scan turns to mush when you zoom in.

/web-resources/movies.title: Movies Glossary
/web-resources/movies.subtitle: Plain-language definitions for the movie terms used across this site and beyond.

terms.def: A copy filmed inside a cinema with a camera or phone. The first leak of a new release, and the worst looking.
An early copy sent to critics and awards voters. Decent quality, but often carries a watermark.
A copy taken straight from a streaming service's own servers. About as clean as a copy gets.
Also from a streaming service, but recorded while it plays rather than taken from the raw file. Slightly below WEB-DL.
A copy taken straight from a Blu-ray disc. The best picture and sound for an older release.
The format used to shrink a video file, like x264 or HEVC. Newer codecs fit the same quality into a smaller file.
A link that tells your torrent app what to download and who to get it from, with no .torrent file needed.
A seeder has the complete file and uploads it, while a leecher is still downloading. More seeders means a faster download.
A server that helps torrent users find each other. Some are open to anyone, others are invite-only.
High Dynamic Range: a wider gap between the darkest and brightest parts of a picture, closer to what your eye sees.
The file type holding the video, audio, and subtitles together, like .mkv or .mp4. The container is the box, the codec is how tightly it is packed.
A synced session where everyone's video plays at the same moment, so a group can watch together from anywhere.
How much data a video uses each second. Higher looks sharper but makes a bigger file.
The pause while the player loads more video, usually because your connection cannot keep up.
The pixel size of a video, like 1080p or 4K. Higher shows more detail.
Softsubs can be turned off or swapped. Hardsubs are burned into the video and cannot be removed.
A backup copy of a site at a different web address, for when the main one is down or blocked.
A block on what you can watch based on your country, caused by licensing deals.
An app that routes your connection through another country, used to get past blocks and add privacy.

/web-resources/music.title: Music Glossary
/web-resources/music.subtitle: Plain-language definitions for the music terms used across this site and beyond.

terms.def: A hacked Spotify app that unlocks Premium features for free. It can break with any update and may get your account flagged.
Tech that splits a finished song back into vocals, drums, bass, and instruments. It is how karaoke tracks and mashups get made.
How much data is packed into each second of audio. Higher sounds richer but makes bigger files, and 320kbps is the usual sweet spot for MP3.
Formats like FLAC that keep every detail of the original recording, unlike MP3. You need decent headphones to hear the difference.
A tool that saves just the audio from a YouTube video as an MP3 file.
Downloading files straight from other people's computers instead of one central server. Soulseek is the classic example for rare music.
The song title, artist, and album art stored inside an MP3 file. Good tags are why your library looks tidy instead of a mess.
Digital Rights Management: the copy protection that stops you saving or sharing music from official apps.
Grabbing a whole album or playlist at once instead of one track at a time.
Original Pilipino Music: Filipino songs and artists across every genre, from ballads to hip hop.
A dark, bass-heavy style of trap built on chopped-up old samples and cowbells. It blew up through car and drift videos.
Using exactly the right song at exactly the right moment in a video for effect.
The pause while a track loads more data because your connection cannot keep up.
A backup copy of a site at a different web address, for when the main one is blocked.
A block on what you can play based on your country, caused by licensing deals.
An app that routes your connection through another country, making it look like you are browsing from there.

/web-resources/parcode.title: Coding Glossary
/web-resources/parcode.subtitle: Plain-language definitions for the coding terms used across this site and beyond.

terms.def: Explaining your code out loud, line by line, to anything sitting on your desk. Saying it slowly usually makes you spot the bug yourself.
Code so tangled that following the logic is a nightmare. It usually comes from rushing without a plan.
The folder holding your whole project plus its full history of changes. Sites like GitHub host these so you can work from anywhere.
A saved snapshot of your changes, tagged with a short note about what you did.
A request asking a project's owners to add your changes. It is also where they review your code first.
Your own copy of someone else's project, so you can experiment without touching theirs.
When two people change the same lines and the tool cannot tell which version to keep. You have to pick by hand.
The same setup code you write at the start of every project before the real work begins.
Integrated Development Environment: one app for writing, running, and fixing your code.
An online space where you can write and run code instantly, with nothing to install.
A ready-made structure that decides how your project is organized, and you fill in the rest.
Someone else's code you drop into your project to save yourself the work.
A tool that installs and updates the outside code your project depends on.
Any outside code your project needs to work. If it breaks, your project breaks with it.
Application Programming Interface: the rules that let one program talk to another, like your app asking a weather service for a forecast.
One specific web address on an API that you send a request to.
The address your computer uses to talk to itself. A site you are testing runs there, visible only to you.
Working on both the part users see and the server and database behind it.
Building a site so it rearranges itself to look right on any screen, from a phone to a big monitor.
Putting your finished project online where anyone can visit it.
An automatic pipeline that tests your code and puts it live every time you save changes.
Code anyone can read, use, and improve for free, because it is published publicly.

/web-resources/torrents.title: Torrenting Glossary
/web-resources/torrents.subtitle: Plain-language definitions for the torrenting terms used across this site and beyond.

terms.def: A link starting with magnet: that tells your torrent app what to find and pulls it from other people, with no file to download first.
Someone who has the complete file and is uploading it to others. More seeders means a faster download.
Someone still downloading who has not finished yet. Everyone is one for a while.
Everyone sharing a torrent right now, seeders and leechers together. You pull pieces from all of them at once.
The app that actually does the downloading, such as qBittorrent or Transmission.
A server that keeps a list of who is sharing a torrent and connects you to them.
Distributed Hash Table: a way for your app to find other sharers without any central tracker.
A small file holding the instructions for a download rather than the content itself. You open it in a torrent client to start.
An invite-only torrent community that usually expects you to keep sharing to stay a member.
How much you have uploaded compared to how much you have downloaded. Private trackers expect you to keep it healthy.
How alive a torrent is, judged by its seeder and leecher counts. Plenty of seeders means a fast download.
A re-released torrent that fixes a mistake or shrinks the file size.
One torrent holding a whole TV season instead of an episode at a time.
An app that routes your traffic through another server, hiding your real location and IP from others.
A block based on your location. Some countries block torrent sites, which is why mirrors and VPNs are common.
A backup copy of a site at a different web address, still working when the main one is blocked.
How many pixels wide and tall a video is, like 1080p or 4K. Higher is sharper but a much bigger download.
How much data is used per second of video or audio. Higher usually means better quality and a larger file.
An exact copy of a whole disc saved as one file, which you can mount or burn later.
The format used to compress video or audio, like H.264 or HEVC. Your player has to support it to play the file.

/web-resources/fun.title: Fun & Creative Glossary
/web-resources/fun.subtitle: Plain-language definitions for the web toy, design and animation terms used across this site and beyond.

terms.def: A small interactive thing made to play with in your browser, with no goal or score.
A hidden joke, reference or surprise tucked into a game, site or scene.
A desktop or phone background that moves, usually a short looping video or animation.
Making an image bigger while an AI fills in the missing detail, so it stays sharp instead of blurry.
Content built by rules and randomness instead of by hand, like a town that shapes itself as you click.
An angled top-down view where nothing shrinks with distance, common in city builders and pixel art.
A key moment you set in an animation; the software fills in the frames between them.
A plain green background that video editors can cut out and replace with anything.
A to-scale, top-down drawing of a building's rooms, walls and doors.
Lining up a scanned old map with real coordinates so it can be laid over a modern map.

/web-resources/web-games.title: Web Gaming Glossary
/web-resources/web-games.subtitle: Plain-language definitions for the browser game, chess, and cubing terms used across this site and beyond.

terms.def: A simple browser multiplayer game you can start instantly, with no download or account. Named after the .io web address most of them use.
A mode where everyone drops into one map and fights until a single player is left.
Coming back into the game after you die, usually somewhere else on the map.
How long your game takes to reach the server, in milliseconds. High ping feels laggy and delayed.
Closing the game in frustration after a bad loss or an unlucky death.
A chess move that is a serious mistake and can hand over the game.
A chess move where one piece attacks two enemy pieces at once, so only one can be saved.
A chess move where the king slides two squares toward a rook and the rook hops over it. Usually done early to keep the king safe.
A pawn capture you can only make right after an enemy pawn moves two squares past yours, and only on your very next move.
A number showing how strong a chess player is. Beating someone rated higher gains you more points.
How much time each player gets for the whole game. Bullet is under 3 minutes, blitz is 3 to 10, rapid is longer.
A timed mode where you solve as many chess puzzles in a row as you can.
The World Chess Federation, which runs official chess rules, titles, and world championships.
A set sequence of moves that mixes up a Rubik's Cube, so every solver starts from the same fair position.
A memorized sequence of moves that solves one part of the cube without breaking what you already did.
Personal best: your fastest solve time ever.
Average of 5: do five solves, drop the fastest and slowest, and average the middle three.
First Two Layers: the step where you build the bottom two layers of the cube at the same time.
The last two steps of the most popular solving method. OLL turns the top face the right way up, then PLL slides those pieces into place.
